props.title: X: The Man with the X-Ray Eyes
props.initialSlug: The power to see all, the price to pay.

sections.content: Roger Corman's X: The Man with the X-Ray Eyes stands as a masterpiece of B-movie psychological horror, starring Ray Milland as Dr. James Xavier, a scientist whose experimental eye drops give him escalating penetrative vision. The film transcends its modest budget through intelligent exploration of scientific hubris and forbidden knowledge, themes later echoed in films like Altered States (1980) and From Beyond (1986). Corman's direction creates genuine unease as Xavier's enhanced vision becomes a curse, moving from seeing through clothes to flesh to the very fabric of reality itself.

sections.content: The film's visual effects, while dated, effectively convey Xavier's increasingly disturbing perspective. Corman employed innovative techniques including infrared photography and solarization to represent X-ray vision, influencing later films like Predator (1987) and They Live (1988) in their representation of altered perception. The progression of Xavier's vision - from medical utility to cosmic horror - creates a compelling narrative arc that examines the price of forbidden knowledge.

The religious undertones become more pronounced as the film progresses, culminating in a shocking finale that echoes Matthew 5:29: "If your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out." This theme of scientific advancement conflicting with divine limits appears in later films like Pi (1998) and The Fly (1986), where human ambition leads to transformation and destruction. sections.content: X: The Man with the X-Ray Eyes helped establish a subgenre of scientific horror focused on enhanced human perception. Its influence can be seen in films like Lucy (2014) and Limitless (2011), where expanding consciousness leads to both power and peril. The film's practical effects and philosophical questions about the nature of reality and human limitations continue to resonate.
